description:
Dinoco Studios is a 2-person team. 

Pratham (Data & AI/Backend): built the satellite pipeline on Microsoft Planetary Computer (Copernicus DEM, Sentinel-1, MODIS, HLS), 8-feature extraction, GPU embeddings, the similarity engine, repo and docs. 

Vivek (Frontend & Pitch): built the Next.js app (3D globe, Moon/Mars explorer, mission modes, site cards, Method page), weighted scoring fix, deployment, demo video, slides and submission.
summary: GEOSYM (Geospatial Extractor of Orbital Similarities & Yield Metrics) finds the places on Earth that best match future Moon and Mars base sites, so mission teams know where to safely test rovers, drills, habitats and crews before launch. We filtered Earth to bare ground and ice, then described 63 sites with eight measurable features: slope, terrain ruggedness, two radar roughness values, two temperatures and two mineral indices. Each site is scored against 10 targets, including Malapert Massif near the lunar south pole and Jezero Crater on Mars, with a transparent weighted-distance formula. Five mission modes change the weights, because a rover test and an ice-drill test need different places. An interactive 3D globe shows each target's top 10 Earth twins, and every site card explains why it matches, where the analogy breaks down and what to test there. The engine flags 48 candidate sites that are not on NASA's current analog list, three of them in India. Every value is clearly labelled as a satellite measurement or an estimate, so users always know exactly how far to trust each result.
details:
What it does.

GEOSYM is a web app that answers one question for any future Moon or Mars base site: where on Earth should we test? A user picks one of 10 targets: five on the Moon (Shackleton Crater Rim, Malapert Massif, Marius Hills Lava Tube Pit, Aristarchus Plateau, Mare Tranquillitatis) and five on Mars (Jezero Crater, Arcadia Planitia, Mawrth Vallis, Elysium Planitia, Valles Marineris). An interactive 3D globe then lights up that target's 10 closest Earth twins out of 63 scored sites.

How it works.

1. Filter Earth: keep only bare ground and ice using ESA WorldCover, and drop forests, farms, cities and water.

2. Measure 8 features per site: mean slope and terrain ruggedness (Copernicus DEM GLO-30), SAR backscatter roughness and depolarization (Sentinel-1 RTC), diurnal thermal swing and minimum night temperature (MODIS land surface temperature), and ferric iron and basaltic mafic indices (HLS and MODIS emissivity). Moon and Mars targets get the same 8 features from published LRO LOLA/Diviner, MGS MOLA, Odyssey THEMIS and MRO CRISM results.

3. Normalize: every feature is scaled 0 to 1 with fixed physical bounds, so slope and temperature can be compared fairly.

4. Score: Match = 1 − Σ(weight × gap) ÷ Σweight. Five mission modes (Balanced, Rover Mobility, Cryo-Thermal, ISRU Mineralogy, Hazard Autonomy) set the weights, and users can fine-tune them with sliders.

5. Explain: each site card shows why it matches, all 8 features side by side, where the analogy breaks down (gravity, atmosphere, radiation) and an AI-written field-test brief, clearly labelled as AI.

Benefits.

- Turns a slow, expert-only site search into a few clicks.

- Matches sites to the specific test a team needs to run.

- Surfaces 48 candidate sites outside NASA's current analog list, including three in India (Changthang and Spiti Valley in the Himalaya, Dhinodhar in Kutch), which could add closer, cheaper test locations for national and international programs.

Intended impact. Help mission planners, researchers and students shortlist field-test sites before Artemis and future Mars missions, and make analog research more open by showing every number and its source.

Tools and languages.

- Frontend: Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. The globe is drawn with d3 and topojson on a canvas.

- Data pipeline: Python with pystac-client and planetary-computer for the Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC API, plus rasterio, rioxarray, xarray, NumPy, SciPy and pandas.

- ML: scikit-learn, UMAP and HDBSCAN for clustering, and PyTorch with experimental Prithvi-EO-2.0 morphology embeddings on an NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 GPU via Marimo/Molab. The embeddings are computed but not used in the score yet.

- AI briefs: Groq (Llama 3.3).

- Hosting: Vercel, with source on GitHub.

- Hardware: our laptops plus the cloud GPU.

Creativity.

- Mission modes show that "the best analog" depends on the mission.

- A playground lets anyone watch a score being built feature by feature.

- Every card is honest about where Earth can't stand in for the Moon or Mars.

Factors we considered.

- Data honesty: slope, ruggedness and the two radar features are satellite measurements for 54 sites. Temperature and mineral values, and all features for 9 sites where extraction failed, are estimates in this build, and the app badges each one.

- Validation: we tested the method against 15 known NASA analogs. They rank in the top half about as often as chance (48% in Balanced mode across all targets), because NASA also picks analogs for logistics and specific science. So we present GEOSYM as a screening tool, not a final verdict.

- Limits of any Earth site: none reproduces Moon or Mars gravity, atmosphere or radiation.

- Accessibility and usability: the app works on phones, supports reduced motion, and uses colour plus text labels.

- AI disclosure: parts of the frontend code were written with Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the team.
